summary:
StayHard is an agentic web platform for exploring NASA’s microgravity combustion research. We built it on open NASA PSI (Physical Sciences Informatics) data. Four ISS studies are analysed in depth, with the other PSI studies available for search. They cover droplet combustion, cool flames, gas flames, solid-material burning and fire safety.

We turned the raw archives (tables, time series, documents, video) into one queryable database. We also built a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) system over the research documents. It uses local embeddings, hybrid vector plus keyword search and cross-encoder reranking. On top of this we built an interactive web app with test explorers, comparisons, charts and 3D simulations that replay experiments from the real data. A Claude-powered agent answers questions only from tool output. It queries the data, retrieves passages through RAG and can pull extra data, such as camera frames, from PSI. Every claim cites its source: test, file, page or DOI. When data is missing, the agent says so. Anything we compute ourselves is labelled as an estimate.

This matters because decades of costly ISS research sit in formats few people can explore. StayHard makes them accessible to researchers, students and the public, without inventing numbers.
details:
What it does

StayHard lets anyone explore NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments without digging through raw archives. Users can browse tests, filter them, compare them side by side, read charts built from real measurements, and watch 3D simulations that replay an experiment from its data. They can also ask the built-in SI agent questions in plain language.

How it works

  • Data. We collected open NASA PSI snapshots for six ISS studies: FLEX, CFI, ACME CFI-G, BASS-II, SAME-R and Saffire-II. Four are analysed in depth. A reproducible offline pipeline turns them into a single read-only DuckDB database, with one schema per study. The data is never edited by hand and the API never writes to it.
  • Beyond NASA’s own data. We also found scientific papers and theses from other publishers (IEEE, ACS, UC Davis, University of South Carolina and others). They explain how droplet-combustion experiments are measured and modelled: image analysis of burning droplets, kinetic modelling of ignition, and simulations of cool flames built on PSI data. Unlike the raw archives, they help people learn, understand and navigate the studies. We added them to both the RAG system and the website. They are cited as separate sources by DOI or link, kept distinct from NASA’s data. Because of copyright, we link to the original publications instead of redistributing the PDFs.
  • RAG. Study descriptions and documents, including this learning material, are split into chunks and embedded with a local bge-small-en-v1.5 model. Search combines vector similarity with BM25 keyword search, followed by cross-encoder reranking.
  • Agent. A Claude-powered SI agent runs a tool-use loop and streams answers to the browser over SSE. Its tools query and aggregate test data, summarise time series, retrieve documents through RAG, build charts, show camera frames and video, and point the user to the relevant page of the app. It answers only from tool output.
  • 3D simulations. Built with React Three Fiber and driven by the measured data, so what you see matches the numbers.

Trust and scientific rigor

  • Every claim carries a citation (test, file, page or DOI).
  • When data is missing, the agent says so instead of guessing.
  • Values we compute ourselves, such as burning-rate constants, are labelled as estimates.
  • We follow the data’s own rules. For example, “disruption” means self-extinction was not observed, not that the flame would burn forever. We also never mix fiber-supported droplets with free-floating ones.

Benefits and impact

Decades of expensive ISS research sit in formats few people can use. StayHard makes it accessible to researchers, students and the public, and every number can be traced to its source. The added scientific literature helps newcomers understand how the measurements were made and what the results mean. This supports fire-safety research for future spacecraft and gives students a hands-on way to learn combustion science.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Query, React Three Fiber, custom SVG charts.
  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, DuckDB.
  • SI: Claude (Anthropic), local embeddings and reranker.
  • Infrastructure: Docker, GitHub Actions CI/CD, Railway.

What makes it creative

It combines an agent that cites its sources, a retrieval system, real-data 3D simulations and a charting interface in one tool. The agent is part of the interface: it can open the right page, highlight the relevant tests and show the matching camera frame. We also went beyond the official data by adding scientific literature from other publishers. We designed the whole app in one consistent visual style.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: no invented numbers, and clear separation of NASA data, third-party material and our own estimates.
  • Reproducibility: the database is rebuilt from code, and raw snapshots are versioned.
  • Accessibility: open data, a public website and no sign-up.
  • Copyright: we link to third-party publications instead of redistributing them.
  • Cost and speed: embeddings and search run locally, so only the agent calls an external model.

    Source code: https://github.com/MartyniukAleksei/nasa-2026
